experiment.question: How many concurrent flow exporters / flows-per-second can riptide 0.6.6 ingest on a 4-vCPU VM before the first flow is dropped, and is the limit riptide or the kernel UDP socket buffer? And what is the ingestion-to-persistence latency? Where is the sustained ingestion limit, and is it CPU- or config-bound?
experiment.hypothesis: First drop is set by the UDP receive-buffer, not riptide's processing; raising net.core.rmem_max moves the knee far higher.
experiment.claim_class: absolute capacity (generator off-box on monkey-head → valid); burst-shaped load (nl6 phase-aligned exporters) — first-drop is a worst-case synchronized burst, not sustained rate

Peak instantaneous rate absorbed with zero loss

sustained_ingestion_rows_s.note: n/a — socket-buffer-bound before the pipeline is reached

experiment.question: riptide flow-ingest capacity: first dropped flow

workload.generator_scenario: nl6 ipfix fidelity loadtest, N synchronized exporters, rate=1000, 20-30s window

first_drop_exporters.note: no drop through 1000 — ceiling not reached

persist_latency_ms.note: sampled now64()-max(receivedAt) while actively persisting; cross-VM clock skew <0.2ms; async_insert flush dominates

sustained_ingestion_rows_s.note: dead-flat 3,600 rows/s (8 parts/s) — an async-insert cadence, not saturation. During drain riptide java used ~1.1 of 4 cores and ClickHouse ~2.5 of 4; neither CPU-bound, so the limit is insert-config (batch/flush) and tunable with headroom. Bursts far above this are absorbed by the 128MB socket buffer and drained in the gaps; sustained arrival above ~3,600/s would grow backlog until the buffer overflows.

reconciliation.note: 1000 exporters: delivered 256000 = accepted 256000 after drain, zero kernel drops; riptide processing knee not reached

ladder: clean, zero loss (drained) — no processing knee reached

experiment.question: riptide flow-ingest capacity: first dropped flow

workload.generator_scenario: nl6 ipfix fidelity loadtest, N synchronized exporters, rate=1000, 20-30s window

profiling.bound: serialized pipeline, not CPU or ClickHouse — ~1.1 of 4 cores busy; 8-thread pool idle

evidence.insert_granularity: ClickhouseRepository.persist() does one client.insert(...).get() per received packet (~24 rows) — 3600 rows/s = ~150 blocking inserts/s
evidence.pipeline_concurrency: Pipeline.process() runs 7 enricher.get() sequentially then persist per packet; per-thread CPU under load: udp-listener 36%, two pool workers 18%+9%, rest idle
evidence.cpu_headroom: riptide ~1.1/4 cores, ClickHouse ~2.5/4 cores during drain

recommendations.change: Accumulate enriched flows into a size/time-bounded buffer (e.g. 5-10k rows or 200ms) and issue one client.insert per batch instead of one per packet.
recommendations.why: Amortizes the per-insert round-trip, async_insert buffer append, and part formation feeding 4 rollup MVs over far more rows. The code's own note measured inserts/s as the governing metric (56->607 with coalescing); fewer, larger inserts move it further.
recommendations.expected: Largest single gain; likely multi-x. No new hardware.

recommendations.change: Fan Pipeline.process across the existing 8-thread parser pool (or a dedicated worker pool consuming a bounded queue) so packets enrich+insert concurrently.
recommendations.why: The pool exists but sits idle (concurrency ~1). Three of four cores are unused; parallelism converts them to throughput.
recommendations.expected: Up to ~coresx toward CPU saturation, compounding with batching.

recommendations.change: Keep multiple inserts in flight (bounded) rather than await each; run independent enrichers concurrently instead of 7 sequential .get()s.
recommendations.why: Every stage serializes on a round-trip; async_insert already acks fast (wait_for_async_insert=0) so the client blocking is pure latency waste.
Not the bottleneck at 150 inserts/s — the server coalescer keeps up easily; only matters after levers 1-3 raise client-side send rate.
recommendations.expected: Negligible until upstream fixed — included to show where it is NOT.
